beats.narration_text: Hello, this is Liam, in for Bear. Jay-Ann Yin's game is Lane Tactics: archers on a five-lane board, where you win by reaching the enemy's back row. This assignment adds two animations: a flag that loops, and a shot that commits. The prompt on screen is an illustrative reconstruction.

shot.label: Illustrative reconstruction of the Claude interface — not a transcript

props.segment: A Waving Flag and a Committed Shot
props.command: Please use Walker to convert my game design document about Lane Tactics — archers on a five-lane board, simultaneous orders, win by reaching the enemy's back row — into two animations: a goal flag that waves from a sprite sheet, and an archer's shot that moves a rig through startup, active and recovery. Test both, and show me what a headless run cannot.

beats.narration_text: One clip loops, one commits. The flag tells a new player where the goal is. It's a found sheet, played by a frame track. The shot tells you who is shooting, and when: a rig of three parts cut from the archer's drawing, moved by keys. Startup, active, recovery: twelve, twenty-one and fifteen frames.
beats.role_note: Setup: the two clips, their jobs, routes, the sheet's licence, the phase lengths (CHANGE-BRIEF §1, §4).

beats.narration_text: A clip is a list of keys, not a movie. This one keys a single integer: the sprite's frame, line seventeen. Four keys, an eighth of a second apart, and the step is one frame period at eight frames a second. The length is half a second, four intervals, so there's no key at the end: the last frame is three, and the wrap goes straight back to zero. Which picture is frame three? The slicing decides, not the image.

beats.narration_text: The read-back test reads the clip back against the brief. Line one seventy-three: every frame key has to be a cell the sheet actually has, fewer than horizontal times vertical frames. Why test that? A key for a cell that doesn't exist loads without a word.

props.title: test_flag_readback.gd: frame range
props.code:
var n_cells: int = sprite.hframes * sprite.vframes
	var inside: bool = not fk.is_empty()
	var ints: bool = true
	var values: Array[int] = []
	for k: Array in fk:
		ints = ints and typeof(k[1]) == TYPE_INT
		var v: int = int(k[1])
		values.append(v)
		inside = inside and v >= 0 and v < n_cells
	rep.check("every frame key is an int", ints)
	rep.check("every frame key is inside the sheet (0 <= frame < hframes x vframes = %d)" % n_cells,
			inside, values)
	rep.check("frame order 0, 1, 2, 3", values == FRAME_ORDER, values)
output: Key times compared within half a frame, never ==

beats.narration_text: Break it on purpose, in a throwaway copy. Key a fifth cell: the game would show a blank frame with no error, and the test fails on exactly that check. Turn the loop off: the flag would wave once and stop, and the loop-mode check fails. And on the first try, the fifth cell also crashed a later check in the test. That index is now guarded.

beats.narration_text: Feel is designed in frames. The game already fixes how long a shot takes: point two seconds to draw, point three five while the arrow flies, point two five to recover. At sixty frames a second: twelve, twenty-one, fifteen. Jay-Ann measured a slow-motion archer, frame by frame, to space the motion inside each phase. The real archer holds at full draw for longer than the whole of our shot. The game skips that. Jay-Ann put the bow drop at frame forty, by eye.
beats.role_note: The phase table (CHANGE-BRIEF §4; revisions 1 and 4). The reference video is not shown.
beats.duration_note: voice 23.125s + lead 0.0s, padded with silence to 718 frames = 718/30 s

beats.narration_text: The table becomes keys. Line thirty-three: the step is one sixtieth. The default is one thirtieth, and frame thirty-three falls between two of those. Line forty-one: a key at every boundary, each time a frame divided by sixty. Three tracks move the rig: the whole archer recoils, the upper body leans, and the bow turns at the hand.

beats.narration_text: One shot at real speed, then at a quarter. Startup: the archer leans back and the bow comes up level. The arrow leaves. Jay-Ann's check: all distinct.

beats.narration_text: One authority: exactly one thing writes each animated node. The clip writes the rig's three pivots, and nothing else. Only the piece script starts it: when the pose becomes draw, line one thirteen looks up its clip, line one fifteen plays it, and line one sixteen applies frame zero at once. Line one twelve stops the last one first, so no old pose carries over. Facing lives one node up, so the clip and the script never touch the same node.

beats.narration_text: Two clocks. A player can advance on the process tick, or the physics tick, or not on its own at all. This one is manual. Line one eighty-two: the piece advances it by the game's own time, from inside the game's update. So when the game pauses, the clip stops. The flag's player is different: it runs on the process tick, in real time.

beats.narration_text: Paused: the archers freeze, the flag keeps waving. That's by design: wind isn't part of the game. And the two clocks agree to within a frame. On the arrow's first frame, the clip is exactly point two seconds ahead of the arrow: one sixtieth of a second ahead of the cue clock, because it advances right after the cue, in the same frame. No physics tick anywhere.

beats.narration_text: The rig's read-back resolves every track to a real node and property. It branches on track type: a 3D transform track names a bone, not a property, so a plain check would call every bone track broken. Here, a value track has to name a property the node really has, line ninety-nine.

beats.narration_text: Rename one property in the clip, a single letter, and in the game the upper body would just stop leaning. No error, no warning: a track that points at nothing is silently inert. The read-back names the track and the missing property. Mutation four empties the import cache, and this one passes, as predicted: the rig is keyed in text, so no import setting can be lost.

beats.narration_text: Strips are where the motion gets judged. Jay-Ann watched the first strip before Claude read it, and wrote: the bow seems to leave the archer's hand. Claude found why: the bow turns at the hand, but the rig cuts the drawing at one column, so the forearm and the string stay behind. One change: the bow's last key, line sixty-eight, from twenty degrees to eight.

beats.narration_text: One hundred two out of one hundred two. Two findings on the way. One frame before the draw, the game is still waiting for the attack order: there, Enter is the order itself, so the first version of the test was wrong, and was fixed to match the game. And the game's own cues land a frame early or late, so the end pose shows for zero or two frames. Game timing was out of scope, so that stays as it is. None of this draws a single pixel.

beats.narration_text: Who did what. Jay-Ann chose both clips, the sheet and the reference, measured its frames, wrote the phase table, the predictions and the answers, captured every strip, and judged every one, including the human checks. Claude agents, working from the brief, wrote the clips, the read-backs and the wiring. Claude Code reviewed them, wrote the pins, the edge tests and the preview, and made the one tuning change Jay-Ann approved. Caught on the way: a recovery split that fell outside the clip, a capture folder that didn't exist, and an author email in a transcript, removed before anything was pushed. The flag sheet is by Fokko, CC0. Source shown: tag a7.
beats.role_note: Human and AI contributions (SOURCES.md A7), mistakes caught (FRICTIONAL A7), the sheet's licence.
beats.duration_note: voice 34.063s + lead 0.0s, padded with silence to 1040 frames = 1040/30 s

beats.narration_text: Verdict. Checked: every track resolves, every key sits on its frame, both loop modes and the frame range are pinned, three mutations fail their tests and the fourth passes for the right reason, the pins didn't move, and a hundred and two edge cases hold. Wrong: where Claude's rig cut the drawing, which split the bow from the hand at twenty degrees, and a frame-before-the-draw assumption in a test. Uncertain: why the game's cues land a frame off, and the recoil, still about a pixel and a half on screen. In Jay-Ann's words: every test was followed by a human check. Next: make the release readable.

Uncertain: why the game's cues land ±1 frame · the recoil, about 1.5 screen px.

In Jiean's words: I chose and measured the exact number of adjustment, and predicted the possible failure to avoid. I approved most of the adjustments suggesstions by Claude. Every test were followed by my own human check.
Next step: make the release readable; predict it first.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. One key, and a prediction first. Here's a prompt to start with: raise the recoil at frame thirty-three from six to eighteen pixels in the art; before changing anything, predict how far that moves on screen, and on which strip frames. Then capture a strip and compare. If the release still doesn't read, that isn't a failure. That's a finding. I'm Liam, in for Bear.
